title: Judges 8:29–35
context: Judges 8:29–35 closes Gideon’s story and prepares for chapter 9. Gideon returns home, has many wives and seventy sons, and a son named Abimelech by his concubine in Shechem. He dies at a good old age and is buried at Ophrah. As soon as he is dead, Israel turns again to the Baals, adopting Baal Berith as their god, and forgets both the LORD who delivered them and the kindness owed to Gideon’s house. The section follows the pattern announced in 2:19, “when the judge was dead, they turned back,” and sets the stage for Abimelech’s bloody bid for kingship (9:1–5).

verses.text: Jerubbaal the son of Joash went and lived in his own house.
verses.arminianNotes: “Jerubbaal the son of Joash went and lived in his own house.” Arminian readers note that the use of the name Jerubbaal recalls Gideon’s early stand against Baal (6:32), a pointed reminder as the chapter ends with Israel returning to Baal worship.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the simple statement of Gideon’s return home appears consistent with his refusal of kingship, though the following verses show a household that looks increasingly royal. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as a quiet transition into the closing summary of Gideon’s life.

verses.text: Gideon had seventy sons conceived from his body, for he had many wives.
verses.arminianNotes: Gideon has “seventy sons conceived from his body, for he had many wives.” Arminian readers note that a large household was a mark of status in the ancient world, and that Gideon’s many wives sit uneasily with Deuteronomy 17:17: “He shall not multiply wives to himself, that his heart not turn away.”
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the seventy sons resemble a royal household, despite Gideon’s refusal of kingship, and they become central to the tragedy of 9:5. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as part of the narrative’s portrait of Gideon’s later life, and both note how it prepares for the conflict in chapter 9.

verses.text: His concubine who was in Shechem also bore him a son, and he named him Abimelech.
verses.arminianNotes: His concubine in Shechem bears a son, and Gideon names him Abimelech. Arminian readers note that the name, commonly understood to mean “my father is king,” stands in tension with Gideon’s words in 8:23. A name chosen by Gideon may suggest a gap between his confession and his aspirations, though the text does not explain his choice.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise note the irony of the name and that Abimelech will seek the very kingship Gideon declined (9:1–6). Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as a foreshadowing of chapter 9, and both caution against claiming more about Gideon’s intent than the text states.

verses.text: Gideon the son of Joash died in a good old age, and was buried in the tomb of Joash his father, in Ophrah of the Abiezrites.
verses.arminianNotes: Gideon dies “in a good old age” and is buried in his father’s tomb at Ophrah. Arminian readers note that the phrase recalls the deaths of the patriarchs, a sign of blessing in a long life. God’s mercy toward Gideon continued despite his failings.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that Gideon’s peaceful death contrasts with the turmoil that follows, and that Hebrews 11:32 names him among those who acted “through faith.” Shared ground: both traditions read Gideon as a real but flawed servant of God, whose faith Scripture honors while his failures are recorded honestly.

verses.text: As soon as Gideon was dead, the children of Israel turned again and played the prostitute following the Baals, and made Baal Berith their god.
verses.arminianNotes: “As soon as Gideon was dead,” Israel turns to the Baals and makes “Baal Berith their god.” Arminian readers note how quickly the people abandon the LORD once their leader is gone. Their choice is real and their own, a pattern of covenant unfaithfulness repeated throughout Judges.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that this fulfills the pattern of 2:19: “when the judge was dead, they turned back.” Baal Berith reappears in 9:4, connected with Shechem. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as showing the depth of Israel’s spiritual instability and the need for a lasting deliverance that no judge could provide.

verses.text: The children of Israel didn’t remember the LORD their God, who had delivered them out of the hand of all their enemies on every side;
verses.arminianNotes: The people “didn’t remember the LORD their God, who had delivered them out of the hand of all their enemies on every side.” Arminian readers note that forgetting God is a moral failure, not merely a lapse of memory. Israel had witnessed his deliverance yet chose not to remember it.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers emphasize that forgetting God is at the root of idolatry. Scripture repeatedly calls God’s people to remember his acts, as in Deuteronomy 8:18: “you shall remember the LORD your God.” Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as a warning that God’s past mercies must be remembered and celebrated, or his people will drift into idolatry.

verses.text: neither did they show kindness to the house of Jerubbaal, that is, Gideon, according to all the goodness which he had shown to Israel.
verses.arminianNotes: Israel did not “show kindness to the house of Jerubbaal, that is, Gideon, according to all the goodness which he had shown to Israel.” Arminian readers note that ingratitude toward God goes together with ingratitude toward people. The failure prepares for the massacre of Gideon’s sons in 9:5.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the verse links forgetting God (8:34) with failing to honor those he used for their good. Both are failures of covenant loyalty. Shared ground: both traditions read the closing verse as a sober summary of Israel’s condition, and both see in Gideon’s story a God who remains faithful even when his people and their leaders fail.
